text.p: The following are the main stories from Wednesday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- Criticism for Lower Saxony state premier Gerhardt Schroeder from the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) executive for his concentration on the interests of his state and his own popularity.
- Former Mecklenburg-Vorpommern interior minister Rudi Geil named as new minister for the development of eastern Germany.
- Complaint by the environmentalist Greens against plans for Garzweiler II, set to be Europe's biggest brown coal mine, rejected by state court.
- Foreign Minister Klaus Kinel sets off for trip to Romania and Slovakia.
- President of the Federation of German Industry (BDI) Hans Olaf Henkel calls on Bonn for more courage to push through vital economic reforms.
HANDELSBLATT
- Thyssen AG and Veba AG interested in taking over bankrupt shipyard group Bremer Vulkan Verbund AG .
- State court rejects complaints against Garzweiler coal mine.
- German DAX index of 30 leading shares climbs above 3,400 points.
- SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine would be in favour of lowering the top rate of tax on private income from 53 percent if the cut was financed by reducing other tax benefits.
- Federal Statistics Office says exports climbed faster than imports in February, up 7.8 percent on the same period last year at 67.8 billion marks.
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG
- Germany and France set to campaign for international ban on human cloning.
- Row in the opposition SPD over what strategy to follow for tax reform. Possible power struggle between Lower Saxony premier Schroeder and SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine.
- German prosecutors drop charges of espionage against legendary East German spymaster Markus Wolf.
- Court rejects Greens criticism of Garzweiler II coal mine.
- Federal court rules that people who commit offences under the influence of alcohol should not automatically have more lenient punishment because of drinking.
- Deutsche Telekom wants to extend its cable television network to make more room for more programmes.
DIE WELT

- Government and opposition signal that a compromise could be reached in the debate over tax refom -- Chancellor Helmut Kohl does not rule out further negotiations and SPD seem to be ready to compromise over the top rate of tax.
- State court rejects complaint against Garzweiler coal mine.
- Experts give a clear "no" to the cloning of humans.
